src: The radial acceleration relation is the fundamental correlation governing late-type galaxy radial dynamics, such that explaining it is necessary and sufficient to account for their in-disc dynamics.

All galaxy types follow a universal radial acceleration relation with a critical acceleration scale of ~10^-10 m/s^2 and remarkably small scatter (~0.13 dex), functioning as a natural law where the baryonic distribution determines the rotation curve.

Weak gravitational lensing around isolated galaxies reveals circular velocity curves that remain flat out to ~1 Mpc, with flat circular speeds following the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation across both early- and late-type galaxies.

The baryonic Tully-Fisher relation is extremely tight (~6% orthogonal intrinsic scatter) when using the mean velocity along the flat part of the rotation curve, with a best-fitting slope of ~3.85, and that the BTFR is more fundamental than the angular momentum-mass (Fall) relation.

A universal radial acceleration relation exists across 153 rotationally supported galaxies, in which the total acceleration (including the dark matter contribution) is fully specified by the baryonic acceleration, constituting a natural law for rotating galaxies.

Gas-rich galaxies fall precisely on the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with scatter attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law governing galaxy dynamics.

Extremely low mass galaxies deviate from the Baryonic Tully-Fisher relation defined by bright galaxies, and that scaling the baryonic mass of faint galaxies—consistent with models where dwarfs have a large fraction of missing baryons—can tighten the relation, though a faint-end break remains subject to systematics.

The relation between dark matter halo mass and baryonic observables (luminosity and stellar mass) follows power laws with steeper slopes for red galaxies (~1.3) than for blue galaxies (~1.0–1.1), and that blue galaxies reside in less clustered environments.

Including gas mass reveals the Tully-Fisher relation to be a single linear relation between total baryonic disk mass and circular velocity of the form Md ∝ Vc^4, holding over five decades in stellar mass.
The baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, calibrated with gas-dominated galaxies, has a slope of approximately 4 and a zero point consistent with stellar population synthesis models.

Properly accounting for systematic uncertainties in galaxy parameters reveals an underlying radial acceleration relation with a characteristic acceleration scale a0 ≈ 1.19 × 10^-10 m/s², intrinsic scatter ≈ 0.034 dex, and weak evidence for the external field effect.

The radial acceleration relation (RAR) inferred from weak-lensing data smoothly continues the kinematic RAR over about 2.5 dex in acceleration, and that early- and late-type galaxies lie on the same joint RAR when consistent isolation criteria and mass estimation methods are applied.

In late-type discs, this one-dimensional relation is the strongest projection of the radial dynamical parameter space and cannot be tightened by adding mass, gas fraction, radius, or other independent properties, with residuals dominated by observational uncertainty [1,2,5]. The RAR also subsumes and generalizes classical scaling relations such as the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation, whose tightness depends crucially on using total baryonic rather than stellar mass [2,4,9,10]. A transition from the Newtonian to a non-Newtonian regime occurs near a critical acceleration of order \(10^{-10}\) m s\(^{-2}\), with little dependence on other global or local galaxy parameters [2,11]. Weak-lensing analyses extend this behaviour to halo scales, showing flat circular speeds and, with consistent mass estimates, that early- and late-type galaxies lie on the same RAR [3,12]. Consequently, explaining the statistics of rotating-galaxy dynamics reduces to explaining the RAR and its minimal intrinsic scatter [1,2,11].

The baryonic Tully–Fisher citations are generally well combined, though [9] and [10] better support the role of total baryonic mass rather than directly proving that the RAR subsumes those relations.

paragraph: Observations of rotating galaxies reveal that their dynamics are governed by a tight empirical relation between the baryonic mass distribution and the total gravitational acceleration — the radial acceleration relation (RAR) [1,2,5]. This relation holds across dwarf, spiral, and early-type galaxies, with remarkably small intrinsic scatter and residuals that do not correlate with any other galaxy property, implying that once the baryonic contribution is known, the full rotation curve follows [2,5,11]. The RAR also underlies and generalizes other scaling laws such as the Tully-Fisher and baryonic Tully-Fisher relations, with baryonic mass scaling approximately as the fourth power of the flat rotation speed [4,6,9,10]. Gravitational lensing studies extend the same relation to much larger radii and lower accelerations, showing that it holds for both early- and late-type galaxies and that circular velocity curves remain flat out to roughly a megaparsec [3,12]. Thus, the dynamics of rotating galaxies are effectively determined by the observed baryons: any additional mass component or modified gravity must be specified by the same single acceleration relation, which poses a challenge to standard cosmological galaxy-formation models [1,6].

The other sources are combined appropriately, since [1,2,5] justify the RAR's fundamentality, while [4,6,9,10] support the BTFR slope and its connection to the RAR.
conflict_answer: Yes, there are tensions. [7] reports that faint dwarf galaxies deviate from the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation and may require large fractions of missing baryons, whereas [2], [5], and [9] find a single, tight baryonic relation that holds across the full mass range. There is also a deeper theoretical conflict: [1] and [6] argue that the RAR and BTFR are naturally explained by modified gravity and challenge standard cosmology, while [8] explicitly assumes standard cosmological dark matter halos and models halo mass–baryon scaling relations without invoking such alternatives. Finally, [3] notes flat rotation curves beyond expected virial radii of dark matter halos, which is difficult to reconcile with the halo-model assumptions in [8].

The radial acceleration relation (RAR) inferred from weak-lensing data smoothly continues the kinematic RAR over about 2.5 dex in acceleration, and that early- and late-type galaxies lie on the same joint RAR when consistent isolation criteria and mass estimation methods are applied.

The mass discrepancy in spiral galaxies correlates most strongly with central surface brightness (a proxy for acceleration), creating fine-tuning problems for dark matter interpretations.

Across spiral and low-surface-brightness galaxies, baryonic mass and rotation velocity follow the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation, while radial acceleration data show that inner kinematic acceleration and outer gravitational acceleration lie on a smooth, shared relation [3,6]. In low-surface-brightness disks, the mass discrepancy is especially large and correlates tightly with low central surface brightness, suggesting that baryonic surface density strongly controls the gravitational response [4,7]. These systems are also gas-rich and slowly evolved, with rotation curves that rise more slowly than those of higher-surface-brightness galaxies and often remain increasing at the outermost radii [4]. Cosmological simulations indicate that low-surface-brightness galaxies arise from the same early progenitors as ordinary spirals, but enhanced star formation, supernova feedback, and later tidal or ram-pressure effects broaden their stars and heat or remove gas [5]. Together, these results imply that spiral and low-surface-brightness galaxy formation and dynamics are shaped by early star formation and feedback, baryonic surface brightness, and a tight coupling between baryonic mass and gravitational acceleration, leaving the relative role of dark matter and modified low-acceleration gravity as a central interpretive issue [2,3,5,6,7].

'cosmic web stripping'—ram-pressure removal of gas from low-mass halos by the moving cosmic web—can explain the scarcity of dwarf galaxies relative to the numerous low-mass dark matter halos predicted in ΛCDM, without invoking feedback or reionization.

The splashback feature—a steepening of the density profile at the first orbital apocenter of accreted matter—is detected in both galaxy density and weak lensing mass profiles around galaxy clusters, consistent with ΛCDM simulations.
The mass-discrepancy acceleration relation emerges naturally from galaxy formation in cold dark matter halos, so it does not require modified dynamics.
Cored dark matter density profiles fit the Fornax dwarf galaxy significantly better than the cuspy halos predicted by cold dark matter simulations.
Dynamical friction timescales are significantly shorter in MOND than in equivalent Newtonian dark-matter systems, posing a challenge to MOND's viability in explaining the Fornax dwarf spheroidal.

Galaxy dark matter halos are flattened and aligned with the stellar light distribution, consistent with cold dark matter simulations, and that alternative gravity theories without dark matter are excluded at 99.5% confidence.

The Walker–Peñarrubia method for inferring dwarf galaxy halo density profiles can falsely detect cores in cuspy NFW dark matter haloes, primarily because the assumed spherical symmetry is violated by elongated and misaligned stellar populations.
Dissipative dark matter density profiles, including mirror dark matter, can reproduce the observed radial acceleration relation.
The Einasto profile is a continuous limiting case of cored double power-law profiles, and that dark matter halos fitted by the Einasto and NFW profiles are not qualitatively distinguishable.

Cold dark matter subhalos are the most likely perturbers to explain observed flux ratio anomalies in strongly lensed systems, supporting the presence of numerous subhalos in lens galaxies as predicted by CDM simulations.

The dark matter density profile of cluster MS 2137−23 has a remarkably flat inner slope (β < 0.9), ruling out steep inner slopes predicted by cold dark matter simulations at better than 99% confidence.

In ΛCDM, moving filaments and pancakes of the cosmic web can ram-pressure-strip gas from low-mass halos, strongly altering their star-formation histories and helping explain the scarcity and diversity of dwarf galaxies [2]. Simulated galaxies also show a tight radial acceleration relation and a characteristic acceleration scale above which baryons dominate, indicating that baryonic physics imprints the internal dynamics even when the dark matter halo is present [4]. Observed dwarfs such as Fornax appear to have shallow, cored inner density profiles, but simulations of ΛCDM Local Group analogues show that elongated and misaligned stellar subpopulations can mimic such cores in mass estimates [5,8]. More exotic or modified frameworks, including decaying dark matter and dissipative dark matter that reproduce the acceleration relation, can reduce subhalo numbers or adjust inner structure, while MOND faces difficulty with systems such as Fornax [1,6,9]. These results imply that explanations for low-mass galaxies must simultaneously match dwarf kinematics, the abundance and internal structure of subhalos, and the baryon-dominated internal scaling relations observed in small systems.

Otherwise, the use of [1], [2], [5], [6], and [8] appropriately addresses subhalo abundance, cosmic-web stripping, inferred cores, and MOND constraints.
conflict_answer: Yes, there are conflicts, especially between inferred cored or shallow inner profiles and the cuspy NFW/Einasto profiles expected in standard CDM simulations. [5] and [12] report such cores/flat inner slopes, while [10], [11], and [3] support the CDM profile picture, and [8] warns that apparent cores can arise from asphericity. There is also a theoretical tension between modified-gravity/no-dark-matter ideas and lensing/kinematics: [7] excludes isotropic no-dark-matter lensing and [6] highlights MOND’s Fornax challenge, even though [4] and [9] show the radial acceleration relation can be accommodated in CDM or dissipative dark matter.

Q1: Do the theories behind finding [12] (supernova-driven outflows removing dark matter cusps) and finding [2] (baryonic feedback in simulations creating dark matter cores) make compatible assumptions about whether baryonic feedback can transform dark matter cusps into kiloparsec-scale cores in dwarf galaxies?
Q2: Taken together, do [12] and [2] support the conclusion that baryonic feedback processes within ΛCDM can generate kiloparsec-scale dark matter cores in dwarf galaxies, addressing the cusp-core and too-big-to-fail problems without modifying gravity?
paragraph: Observations of dwarf galaxy rotation curves consistently reveal constant-density cores that contradict the steep cusps predicted by dark-matter-only simulations [4], [11]. Within the standard cosmological paradigm, this cusp-core discrepancy is primarily resolved by baryonic feedback processes, specifically supernova-driven gas outflows that transfer energy to the dark matter halo [12]. High-resolution hydrodynamic simulations demonstrate that these outflows can flatten central density profiles in galaxies with sufficient stellar mass, effectively addressing the too-big-to-fail problem [2], [7]. Empirical data from surveys like THINGS and SPARC further support models where halo profiles depend on the stellar-to-halo mass ratio rather than universal cuspy forms [4], [7]. However, the efficiency of this transformation depends on the star formation history and stellar mass, meaning some ultrafaint dwarfs may retain cuspy profiles [2], [12]. Ultimately, incorporating realistic baryonic physics into standard cosmology models reconciles the majority of observational data without requiring modifications to the nature of dark matter [7], [12].
review_answer: Yes, there are significant problems with how the sources are combined to form a consensus. The paragraph presents baryonic feedback as a definitive solution, yet Source [5] explicitly argues that stellar feedback may not be an effective mechanism to flatten central cusps, and Source [3] indicates that dwarf spheroidals favor cusped profiles when using nonspherical models. Consequently, the synthesis ignores significant dissent in the provided literature, portraying an unresolved debate as a settled matter.
conflict_answer: Several sources conflict on whether baryonic feedback can resolve the cusp-core problem, with [2], [4], [7], and [12] arguing supernova-driven outflows create cores, while [5] concludes that mass loss driven by stellar feedback is not effective enough to flatten central cusps. Observational interpretations also diverge, as [1], [4], [8], and [11] find data favors constant-density cores, whereas [3] uses nonspherical models to argue that dwarf spheroidals actually favor cusped profiles. Additionally, while most sources operate within standard ΛCDM, [6] and [10] propose alternative physics like interacting dark energy or decaying dark matter to explain small-scale structure discrepancies.
probe_answer:
Q1: Yes. Both sources operate within the standard ΛCDM framework and attribute the flattening of dark matter profiles to energy injection from supernova-driven gas outflows. They share the fundamental assumption that bursty star formation feedback is capable of transferring sufficient energy to dark matter particles to transform cusps into kiloparsec-scale cores.

Q2: Yes. Both papers explicitly demonstrate through cosmological simulations that supernova feedback can flatten central density profiles enough to resolve observational discrepancies within standard cosmology. Their combined results provide robust theoretical evidence that modified gravity or alternative dark matter models are not strictly necessary to explain these specific small-scale structure problems.

src: MOND predictions based on baryonic mass alone (with no dark matter) are consistent with observed velocity dispersions of Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxies.

MOND with the 'simple' interpolating function successfully fits high-quality THINGS rotation curves, yielding a consistent value of a0 and stellar mass-to-light ratios in agreement with population synthesis models.

MOND's predictions for galaxy-galaxy gravitational lensing—a logarithmic radial potential and a normalization σ = (MGa₀/4)^(1/4)—are confirmed by observations using baryonic mass-to-light ratios, while Newtonian analysis requires a mass discrepancy factor of ~40.

Including tidal evolution is necessary for accurate binary population synthesis, and that initial separations should be distributed according to the observed distribution of semilatera recta rather than periods or semimajor axes.

While MOND significantly reduces the mass of the dark component needed in galaxy clusters, it does not remove it completely, and massive neutrinos are a possible candidate for the remaining dark mass.

Applying MOND to galaxy clusters reduces the virial mass discrepancy from a factor of 4 to about 2, but does not eliminate it, implying that if MOND is correct, additional baryonic matter remains undetected in cluster centers.

Apparent difficulties for MOND in fitting galaxy rotation curves (spread in fitted a0 values and large-radius behavior) can be attributed to methodological issues in Kent's analysis—specifically the omission of H I gas mass and use of averaged asymmetric rotation curves—rather than failures of MOND itself.
MOND reproduces the rotation curves of about 80 galaxies from the observed distribution of baryonic matter alone, with mass-to-light ratios consistent with stellar population synthesis predictions.

MOND-predicted rotation curves are compatible with observed curves for some spiral galaxies at Cepheid-based distances, though MOND prefers somewhat different distances for others (smaller for NGC 3198, larger for NGC 2841).

In MOND theories, AQUAL predicts a weaker external field effect than previously published AQUAL results but a stronger EFE than QUMOND, demonstrating theoretical uncertainties in MOND predictions for disk galaxy rotation curves.

The deep-MOND parameter Q, measured from galaxy rotation curves in the SPARC sample, weakly favors modified gravity over modified inertia theories, though both remain consistent with the data within 1.5σ.

In the Bekenstein-Milgrom formulation of MOND, a simple algebraic relation between the MOND potential and the Newtonian potential holds outside thin-disc galaxy models, enabling efficient computation of MOND rotation curves from Newtonian curves and surface density profiles.

paragraph: Research indicates that modified dynamics theories provide a robust explanation for observed galaxy dynamics without invoking large amounts of dark matter. Studies of galactic rotation curves demonstrate that predicted velocities align closely with observations when using modified gravity formulations based on baryonic mass distributions [2], [7], [8]. Gravitational lensing data further supports this paradigm, showing consistency with logarithmic potential predictions that require significantly lower mass-to-light ratios than Newtonian analysis [3]. While dwarf spheroidals also exhibit velocity dispersions consistent with these theoretical predictions, some tension remains regarding distance estimates in specific spiral galaxies [1], [9]. At the cluster scale, modified dynamics reduces the mass discrepancy substantially, though it may not eliminate the need for some additional dark component entirely [5], [6]. Current investigations continue to refine these models by examining external field effects and distinguishing between modified gravity and inertia formulations [10], [11].
review_answer: The paragraph provides a strong synthesis of the provided literature, though it occasionally conflates the general phenomenological success of modified dynamics with specific modified gravity formulations in the earlier citations. While sources [2] and [8] report strong empirical agreement, grouping source [7] with them glosses over its primary focus on methodological optimizations and addressing previous difficulties rather than confirming agreement. Additionally, labeling the earlier works as "modified gravity" preemptively narrows the distinction between modified gravity and inertia that sources [10] and [11] identify as an ongoing theoretical uncertainty.
conflict_answer: Sources [1], [2], [3], and [8] assert that modified dynamics successfully explains galaxy-scale observations without dark matter, whereas sources [5] and [6] conclude the theory fails to fully resolve mass discrepancies in galaxy clusters without invoking additional dark mass. Additionally, while earlier papers treat the framework as consistent, sources [10] and [11] highlight internal theoretical conflicts regarding whether the phenomenon stems from modified gravity or inertia, noting divergent predictions for effects like the external field effect. Specific tensions also exist regarding individual galaxies, where sources [2] and [9] note distance-related fit issues for objects like NGC 3198 that contrast with the broader success claimed in source [8].

Q1: Yes. Both studies operate under the fundamental assumption that gravitational acceleration is derived directly from the observed baryonic mass distribution using a specific interpolating function. They share the core premise that no dark matter halo is required, relying instead on the modification of dynamics governed by the acceleration constant a0.

Q2: Yes. Both papers explicitly report that the required mass-to-light ratios for successful fits align closely with independent predictions from stellar population synthesis models. Furthermore, each study confirms that the observed rotation curves are well-reproduced using only the detected baryonic matter within the MOND framework.
